content: Heaven's Gate was a religious group led by Marshall Applewhite and Bonnie Nettles. The group believed that the appearance of Comet Hale-Bopp in 1997 signified an opportunity for their souls to ascend to a higher existence. Applewhite convinced 38 followers to commit suicide, asserting that their souls would board a spaceship hidden behind the comet, which they believed was carrying Jesus. This belief system has led some to classify Heaven's Gate as a UFO religion. The group also held that Earth was on the verge of being recycled or renewed, and the only way to escape this fate was to leave the planet immediately. Although the group was formally against suicide, they redefined the term to mean rejecting the Next Level when it was being offered. They viewed their human bodies as mere vehicles for their spiritual journey. Members were taught to detach from earthly existence, often selling their possessions upon joining the group. They believed that hating the material world and their physical bodies was a test of faith, requiring them to leave without tangible proof of the Next Level's existence. Heaven's Gate was founded by Marshall Herff Applewhite and Bonnie Lu Truesdale Nettles before 1975. By the mid-1970s, the pair were known within the group as Bo and Peep or Do and Ti, and collectively as The Two. They claimed to have arrived on Earth via a UFO from a level above human and promised to return through a secretive process taught to their followers. The group never had more than a few hundred members and lost many adherents after Nettles' death in 1985. They were described as a secretive New Age religion and held meetings in various locations, including a hotel on the Oregon coast, before relocating to California. The group lived in isolation in the western United States for many years, often traveling in pairs to recruit new members. At one point, they lived in a darkened house to simulate the experience they expected during their journey through outer space. Much of what is known about the group comes from the research of Robert Balch and David Taylor, who infiltrated the group in the 1970s. Members adopted new names with the suffix -ody, symbolizing their identity as children of the Next Level. This practice was mentioned in Applewhite's final video, Do's Final Exit, recorded on March 19, 1997, shortly before the group's mass suicide. In the months leading up to their deaths, some members worked for a San Diego-based company developing computer-based instruction for the U.S. Army. They were described as polite but reserved and informed their supervisor that they had completed their mission before leaving their jobs. The group also designed websites for themselves and paying clients, including the San Diego Polo Club. One member, Thomas Nichols, was the brother of Star Trek actress Nichelle Nichols. Before the group's suicide, he and other members sought her help in publicizing their message. The structure of Heaven's Gate resembled that of a medieval monastic order. Members renounced material possessions and lived an ascetic lifestyle, sharing everything communally. Six male members voluntarily underwent castration as an extreme measure to maintain their asceticism. The group funded itself through professional website development services. On March 26, 1997, 38 members and their leader, Applewhite, were found dead in a rented mansion in Rancho Santa Fe, California. This mass death is one of the most widely known examples of cult suicide. In preparation, members performed a ritual body cleanse by drinking citrus juices. The suicide was carried out by ingesting phenobarbital mixed with vodka, followed by asphyxiation using plastic bags secured around their heads. They were found lying neatly in bunk beds, with their faces and torsos covered by square purple cloths. Each member carried $5 and a few quarters in their wallets. They were dressed identically in black shirts, sweatpants, brand-new black-and-white Nike sneakers, and armband patches reading Heaven's Gate Away Team. The suicides were conducted in shifts, with remaining members cleaning up after each group. Before their deaths, Heaven's Gate was known within UFOlogical circles and had been the subject of academic studies. Jacques Vallée, in his book Messengers of Deception, described an unusual public meeting organized by the group and expressed concerns about the authoritarian nature of contactee groups like Heaven's Gate. In January 1994, an article in LA Weekly brought the group, then known as The Total Overcomers, to the attention of Rio DiAngelo, who eventually joined them. DiAngelo later became the subject of a 2007 LA Weekly cover story. Louis Theroux contacted the group in early March 1997 for his BBC documentary series but was told they could not participate as it would interfere with their focus at the time.
